item.title: VoroTypes: automated enumeration of Voronoi cell topologies for structural identification of complex crystals in atomistic simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.21911v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: VoroTypes enumerates, for an arbitrary crystal structure, the complete family of Voronoi cell topologies that can arise under small generic perturbations of atomic positions, and exports it as a topological filter for the VoroTop framework. This extends per-atom structural identification in molecular dynamics simulations, previously limited to a handful of simple reference structures, to complex crystals such as Frank--Kasper and Laves phases, with per-sublattice resolution. The package takes a standard crystallographic description (a CIF or POSCAR file) as input, applies exact symmetry reduction and validity pruning to accelerate the enumeration, and produces filters that load directly into the standalone VoroTop program or into OVITO. A library of pre-computed filters covers over a thousand structures from the Materials Project.
item.dc:creator: Emanuel A. Lazar, Chris H. Rycroft

item.title: Self-Scaled Broyden Family of Quasi-Newton Methods in JAX
item.description: arXiv:2603.10599v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a JAX implementation of the Self-Scaled Broyden family of quasi-Newton methods, fully compatible with JAX and building on the Optimistix~\cite{rader_optimistix_2024} optimisation library. The implementation includes BFGS, DFP, Broyden and their Self-Scaled variants (SSBFGS, SSDFP, SSBroyden), as well as L-BFGS, together with a Zoom line search satisfying the strong Wolfe conditions. This is a short technical note, not a research paper, as it does not claim any novel contribution; its purpose is to document the implementation and ease the adoption of these optimisers within the JAX community. The code is available at https://github.com/IvanBioli/ssbroyden_optimistix and on PyPI (pip install ssbroyden-optimistix).
item.dc:creator: Ivan Bioli, Mikel Mendibe Abarrategi

item.title: ANEForge: Python for direct computation on the Apple Neural Engine
item.description: arXiv:2606.17090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: ANEForge is a Python package that programs the Apple Neural Engine (ANE), the fixed-function neural accelerator on every recent Apple device, directly and without CoreML. In production the engine is reachable only through CoreML, which treats it as a scheduling option: no configuration requires the ANE, and a model can silently run on the CPU or GPU instead. ANEForge compiles a lazy tensor graph, built from 58 fused operators and 19 native bridge operators, into a single ANE program. The program is dispatched through the same ANE daemon and kernel-driver stack as Apple's internal framework. Beyond inference, the package reaches the engine's native fused attention, streams int8, int4, and sparse weights, keeps decoder and optimizer state resident across steps, and runs the forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer update of training on the engine. A small fused program completes a call in about 90us, near the engine's 70us per-program dispatch floor, and a pretrained ResNet-18 forward runs end-to-end in 0.33ms. ResNet-18, a sentence encoder, and a Vision Transformer run end-to-end against framework references, and a Stable Diffusion U-Net validates its forward pass. ANEForge targets Apple Silicon under macOS 14 and later. Each release is verified against a recorded macOS and ANE-compiler version.
item.dc:creator: Spencer H. Bryngelson

item.title: CNet: A Complex-Valued Deep Learning Framework with Wirtinger Autodifferentiation and FFT--Hadamard Convolution
item.description: arXiv:2610.08592v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: CNet is a C++/CUDA framework for deep complex-valued neural networks (CVNNs), trained by gradient descent with explicit Wirtinger (CR-calculus) derivatives. Complex models are underexplored yet natural where data is intrinsically complex -- RF/IQ, MRI k-space, radar/SAR, audio spectra -- and phase carries information real networks discard. CNet is physics-native: a network is a cascade of complex (often unitary) operations on an amplitude vector, and classification is a Born-rule measurement p_k = |z_k|^2 / ||z||^2 rather than a softmax over real logits. Every layer ships a CPU reference and a finite-difference-verified CUDA kernel; the static, batch-cloned computation graph captures cleanly into CUDA Graphs, outperforming eager and compiled torch.complex64 on an H100. We present three studies. (1) A fully complex causal language model, built on a new causal (triangular-masked) Fourier mixer with an O(N log N) Bluestein evaluation of the forward pass and its Wirtinger adjoint, matches a parameter-matched real causal FNet on character-level tiny-shakespeare in under half the steps. We introduce Born-rule attention, a content-based causal mixer whose weights are the quantum-measurement probabilities |<Q_k, K_j>|^2 -- to our knowledge the first classical, complex-valued attention to replace softmax with the squared-magnitude Born score; with rotary embeddings and per-token complex normalization it reaches 1.52 nats/char, matching softmax self-attention, and transfers unchanged to byte-level (1.31 nats/char) and sub-word WikiText-103. (2) On radio-modulation classification (RML2016.10a/RML22) we trace the pooled-power accuracy ceiling to discarded temporal structure and recover it with a learnable cyclostationary conjugate-lag operator. (3) A bottleneck analysis of the Fourier phase problem in coherent-diffraction imaging isolates where complex-valued networks still need new operators.
item.dc:creator: Marcel Crasmaru
